towns:Saint-Tropez.name: Saint-Tropez
towns:Saint-Tropez.teaser: Under the yachts, a fortified fishing port that still sells its catch on marble every morning
towns:Saint-Tropez.story: Strip away August and Saint-Tropez is a small fortified port on the south shore of its own gulf, named for Torpes, the martyr whose headless body, legend says, drifted ashore here in a boat. Every May since 1558 the Bravade carries his gilded bust through the streets to drums and musket fire. In the mornings fishermen lay out bream, red mullet and octopus on marble at the fish market behind the quay; on Tuesdays and Saturdays the plane trees of the Place des Lices shade the market, and by afternoon the gravel is a pétanque court again. By mid-October the town is its residents' again.
towns:Saint-Tropez.why: Come on a Saturday morning in autumn: the market under the planes, fish on the slabs, and room to walk the quay.
facts: The old port and its fish market at the Place aux Herbes, the lanes of La Ponche, the Place des Lices market (Tuesday and Saturday, 8am-1pm, all year; Oct 2026) and the boules in the afternoon

towns:Ramatuelle & Gassin.name: Ramatuelle & Gassin
towns:Ramatuelle & Gassin.teaser: Two hill villages above Pampelonne, and an actor's plain grave under a laurel
towns:Ramatuelle & Gassin.story: Pampelonne's sand belongs to Ramatuelle, but the village turns its back on the beach clubs: an old village perched above the vines, its lanes wound in rings round the hill. Gérard Philipe, the actor of Le Cid, spent his holidays at his in-laws' house here and is buried in the village cemetery, near the school that carries his name. The grave, covered in ivy and shaded by a laurel, was kept deliberately one of the plainest there; a regional guide says he was buried in his Cid costume. On the next ridge Gassin is the other perched village, its terrace looking out over the whole gulf of Saint-Tropez.
towns:Ramatuelle & Gassin.why: Stand at Philipe's grave in Ramatuelle, then drive up to Gassin for the gulf at the end of the day.

towns:Bormes-les-Mimosas.name: Bormes-les-Mimosas
towns:Bormes-les-Mimosas.teaser: A medieval village of stairs and covered passages that renamed itself for a flower in 1968
towns:Bormes-les-Mimosas.story: Until 1968 it was plain Bormes; that year the commune added '-les-Mimosas', for the yellow that covers its hills from January to March (where the tree came from is its own card's story). Every February since 1920 a corso fleuri has carried the flower through the streets, first on carts drawn by donkeys, then on tractors, now on floats dressed with some 12 tonnes of mimosa, with a battle of flowers on the Sunday. The rest of the year the old village is stairways and covered medieval passages such as the Ruelle des Sarrazins, climbing above the coast road, with Fort de Brégançon on its rock offshore.
towns:Bormes-les-Mimosas.why: Lose an hour in the stairways of the old village, then eat in a covered medieval lane.

Morning in the lanes; February for the mimosa and the corso (14-15 Feb in 2026, paid entry; book the Sunday)

towns:Toulon.name: Toulon
towns:Toulon.teaser: The Var's capital is a navy port that feeds you honestly, for a third of a Saint-Tropez bill
towns:Toulon.story: Toulon is the Var's capital and a warship town, not a resort: grey hulls in the Rade, sailors on the quays, and tables that cost about a third of what the gulf charges. Walk up from the port into the Basse Ville, the old town, on a market morning and the air smells of chickpea batter: the cade, Toulon's own galette, is baked thin in wide copper pans and sold by the slice from carts along the Cours Lafayette. The town claims a second dish as its own, the sugared fried chichi frégi from the seafront kiosks. Mont Faron rises behind it all (its own walk card).
towns:Toulon.why: Give Toulon a market morning: cade from the cart, a natural wine at noon, and the Rade in front of you.
facts: The Rade and its warships, the old town, Toulon's own street food and the Var's natural-wine counters
Morning, while the Cours Lafayette market runs (Tuesday to Sunday; closed Mondays)
The Cours Lafayette market (its own card); Superbuvette, Les Quilles and La Dégust' Nature for natural wine; the navy, in the curiosity 'Most of the French fleet sleeps in Toulon'

towns:Sanary-sur-Mer & Le Brusc.name: Sanary-sur-Mer & Le Brusc
towns:Sanary-sur-Mer & Le Brusc.teaser: Painted pointus on the quay, rosé at six, and a ten-minute boat to an island
towns:Sanary-sur-Mer & Le Brusc.story: Sanary still works for a living: the pointus, the painted wooden fishing boats of Provence, rock at their moorings along the quay, and the fishermen sell from them in the morning. Just west along the coast, Le Brusc is the fishing harbour of Six-Fours-les-Plages, not of Sanary. From its Quai Saint-Pierre a boat crosses in about ten to twelve minutes to the Île des Embiez, where Paul Ricard, the pastis maker, lies on the island's highest point, looking back at the coast he sold his drink to.
towns:Sanary-sur-Mer & Le Brusc.why: Take the quayside apéritif in Sanary at six, and the Embiez boat from Le Brusc the next morning.

towns:Bandol.name: Bandol
towns:Bandol.teaser: The harbour that shipped Roman wine and lent its name to the Var's greatest red
towns:Bandol.story: Bandol is a harbour town before it is a label. The Romans terraced the slopes behind it and shipped their wine from this port, and the town gave its name to the appellation that now spreads over eight communes, some 70 estates and three cooperatives in the hills behind. Down here is where you taste them side by side, at the appellation's own Maison des Vins. On the first weekend of December the growers come down to the port for the Fête des Vins de Bandol, the new-vintage tasting that makes the coast's warmest winter day out. Offshore sits the small island of Bendor.
towns:Bandol.why: Time it for the December Fête des Vins, when the growers bring the new vintage down to the port.
facts: The port, a side-by-side tasting of the appellation, the island of Bendor
Late morning, tasting before lunch; the first weekend of December for the Fête des Vins

towns:Hyères.name: Hyères
towns:Hyères.teaser: The Riviera's first winter town, all palms, villas and a medieval hill, before the islands
towns:Hyères.story: Hyères was taking winter visitors before most of the coast knew it had a season: it is often called the oldest winter resort of the Côte d'Azur, and the town's own heritage panels describe a 'ville à l'heure anglaise', an English winter town. Queen Victoria came in 1892 (the sources disagree on how long she stayed). The wealthy winterers built villas with acclimatisation gardens and planted the palms that line the boulevards. Behind them the medieval old town climbs its hill in steep lanes, and on Saturday mornings the Grand Marché des Îles d'Or spills along Avenue Gambetta and the Place Clemenceau.
towns:Hyères.why: Do the Saturday market, then climb the medieval lanes of the old town above the palms.
facts: The medieval old town, the palm boulevards and Belle Époque villas, the Saturday market
Saturday morning, from about 7am, for the market; winter, the season the town was built for

towns:Collobrières.name: Collobrières
towns:Collobrières.teaser: The Maures village that calls itself chestnut capital, and proves it three Sundays every October
towns:Collobrières.story: Collobrières sits on its river deep in the Massif des Maures, a stone village ringed by chestnut groves that calls itself the capital of the chestnut. In October it proves it: the Fêtes de la Châtaigne fill three Sundays, in 2026 the 11th (Var producers' day), the 18th (the international day, when twin towns, brotherhoods and Italian flag-throwers parade) and the 25th (old trades and crafts). The rest of the year it is a quiet place of plane trees and an old bridge over the river, with the confectioner's shop facing it. For the record, a marron is a selected large-fruited chestnut, not a separate nut.
towns:Collobrières.why: Go on one of the October Sundays, early, and walk it off on a Maures trail afterwards.
facts: Chestnut country, the old bridge, the start of the best Maures walks (up to La Verne, up to Notre-Dame-des-Anges)

curiosities:The fig with its own appella.name: The fig with its own appellation
curiosities:The fig with its own appella.teaser: France grows one fig with an appellation, and nobody agrees how much of the country's crop it is
curiosities:The fig with its own appella.story: France has exactly one fig with its own appellation: the Figue de Solliès, the near-black Bourjassotte Noire of the Gapeau valley northeast of Toulon. It became an AOC in 2006 and a European AOP in 2011. It is picked from about 15 August into October and sold dead-ripe from the orchards and village stalls of the valley. What it weighs in the national harvest is a number everyone quotes and nobody quite agrees on.
curiosities:The fig with its own appella.why: Eat one in the valley in its last weeks; the larder card tells you where to buy.
facts: Mid-October is the tail of the harvest: the last AOP figs are on the stalls around Solliès-Pont (where to buy is the card 'The Solliès fig growers')

The Ministry of Agriculture says the appellation is 80% of France's fig production; other sources give about three-quarters; a 2025 trade report puts the Solliès basin at two-thirds to three-quarters; the cooperative alone is put at about 60%. curiosities:The cork oak that survives t.name: The cork oak and the fire
curiosities:The cork oak that survives t.teaser: A tree that loses its leaves to a forest fire and puts out green shoots a few weeks later
curiosities:The cork oak that survives t.story: Drive into the Maures and the rock changes under the wheels: this massif is old crystalline schist, not the limestone of the rest of Provence, and its non-limestone soils grow chestnut and cork oak. The cork oak is built for fire. Its thick bark insulates the trunk, so when a blaze runs through, the tree loses its leaves and most of its small branches but the trunk is only scorched; within weeks green shoots break from the blackened limbs. The same bark, stripped from living trees, was the Maures' industry for centuries and corked the bottles of the south.
curiosities:The cork oak that survives t.why: Look at the trunks along the Maures roads: blackened bark with green growth on top is the whole story.
facts: The cork-oak woods around Collobrières and Gonfaron, where the massif's cork trade was based; the Maures burned badly in 2021, and the regrowth is visible from the roads

The State environment office (DREAL PACA) says cork-oak forests recover well only if fires are not too frequent, and abandoned, uncleared stands burn readily: 'survives the fire' holds for one fire, not for repeated ones

curiosities:The mimosa is Australian.name: The mimosa is Australian
curiosities:The mimosa is Australian.teaser: The yellow that defines a Var winter came over the garden walls from Australia
curiosities:The mimosa is Australian.story: The mimosa that turns the Maures yellow every winter is not from Provence at all. Acacia dealbata is Australian: it arrived on the Riviera as a garden plant in the 1800s, escaped over the walls and spread across the hills, until the coast came to think of it as its own. Bormes made the adoption official in 1968, when the commune renamed itself Bormes-les-Mimosas. Its corso began in 1920, with the flowers heaped on carts drawn by donkeys; tractors and then floats took over, and the 2026 parade was billed as the 83rd.
curiosities:The mimosa is Australian.why: Come in February and the import is the most local-looking thing in the Var.
facts: Nothing in flower in October: the trees bloom from January to March, and the corso is in mid-February in Bormes (14-15 Feb in 2026)

The 1920 start is Bormes's own date; a Var tourism page dates Provençal flower corsos generally to the late 19th century, and the old guide's 'oldest flower parade on the Côte d'Azur' was not confirmed

curiosities:Why the islands are golden.name: Why the islands are golden
curiosities:Why the islands are golden.teaser: No treasure: the Îles d'Or are said to take their name from mica flashing in the rock
curiosities:Why the islands are golden.story: The Greeks called them the Stoechades, the islands 'in a row', one behind another: Porquerolles, Port-Cros and Le Levant strung along the horizon off Hyères. The golden name came later, usually dated to the Renaissance, and the usual explanation is the rock, not treasure: the islands are built of mica-schist, and under a low, slanting light the mica glints gold. Hyères keeps a folk tale as well, of a nobleman whose four daughters were famous for their beauty and for swimming off the coast. Neither version rests on a document the sources produce.
curiosities:Why the islands are golden.why: Watch the island shores from the boat late in the day and decide for yourself.
facts: From the boat to Porquerolles or Port-Cros in late-afternoon light, watch the schist of the shore cliffs (the islands trip card owns the ferry)
The Renaissance date and the mica-schist explanation are widely repeated (Routard, regional guides) but no primary source was found; the folk tale of the four daughters is the alternative

curiosities:Most of the French fleet sle.name: Most of the French fleet sleeps in Toulon
curiosities:Most of the French fleet sle.teaser: Over 60% of the French navy's tonnage ties up in one Var roadstead
curiosities:Most of the French fleet sle.story: Toulon's fate was its roadstead, deep and sheltered. Henri IV founded a shipyard here in 1599; Richelieu and then Colbert enlarged it, and Vauban designed the new basin, the darse Vauban. Today the arsenal covers some 268 hectares behind about 10 km of quays: the largest naval base in the Mediterranean and in Western Europe, home port of the carrier Charles de Gaulle and of the navy's nuclear attack submarines, and the berth of more than 60% of the French fleet's tonnage. Its two largest drydocks are given as 422 m by 40 m; work on the 400 m docks began in 1911.
curiosities:Most of the French fleet sle.why: Take the boat round the Rade: the grey hulls are the most permanent thing on this coast.
facts: The arsenal is a military zone; see it from a boat tour of the Rade from Quai Cronstadt on the old port, or from Mont Faron above (its own card)

curiosities:The river the Var lost in 18.name: The river the Var lost in 1860
curiosities:The river the Var lost in 18.teaser: The Var is named for a river that has not flowed through it since 1860
curiosities:The river the Var lost in 18.story: Until 1860 the river Var was a frontier: the department's eastern edge ran along it, with the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia on the far bank. When Nice was annexed that year, France rebuilt the Alpes-Maritimes from the county of Nice and, taken from the Var, the arrondissement of Grasse. The river ended up entirely outside the department, and the Var kept its name anyway, a department named for water that no longer touches it. The same line explains a sandwich: the pan bagnat sold on Var beaches is Niçois, from across a border barely a century and a half old.
curiosities:The river the Var lost in 18.why: Drop it at lunch over a pan bagnat: the department, and the sandwich, belong to two sides of an 1860 border.
facts: Order a pan bagnat on a Var beach and know it is an import: pan banhat, 'bathed bread', in the old Nissart tongue

curiosities:15 August 1944.name: 15 August 1944
curiosities:15 August 1944.teaser: Provence's own D-Day: the landing that freed Toulon and Marseille in under a fortnight
curiosities:15 August 1944.story: Normandy has its D-Day; Provence has 15 August 1944. At 8am Operation Dragoon put Allied troops ashore on beaches between Toulon and Cannes, the main landings strung from Cavalaire to Saint-Raphaël. Some 350,000 men were engaged, about 250,000 of them in General de Lattre de Tassigny's French Army B. The prize was the two great ports, which could then land men and supplies for the drive north: Marseille was freed on 28 August, and Toulon fell in the same last days of the month, under a fortnight after the landing. Provence remembers it as its own liberation.
curiosities:15 August 1944.why: Stand at the memorial on Mont Faron and look down at the port the landing was fought for.
facts: The Mémorial du Débarquement et de la Libération en Provence on the summit of Mont Faron (the cable car belongs to the Mont Faron walk card; check opening); the landing beaches of the Cavalaire bay are in the sister guide at /terroir/Cavalaire-sur-Mer/

Troop numbers: about 350,000 for the operation (Ministry of the Armed Forces), the French share given as 250,000 or 260,000 (Hérodote); the old guide's 'half a million' is not supported. The exact day of Toulon's liberation was not pinned in the sources checked

curiosities:Sanary, capital of German le.name: Sanary, capital of German letters
curiosities:Sanary, capital of German le.teaser: In 1933 a Var fishing port became the capital of German literature in exile
curiosities:Sanary, capital of German le.story: After Hitler took power in 1933, a small fishing port in the Var filled with German-speaking writers. The critic Ludwig Marcuse called Sanary the 'capital of German literature in exile': Thomas Mann and his son Klaus, Lion Feuchtwanger, Franz Werfel and Alma Mahler, Stefan Zweig among those who came. Aldous Huxley was there before them: he bought a house in 1930, wrote Brave New World in it, and from 1933 welcomed the exiles. The war scattered the colony again. A plaque now lists 36 German-language writers and artists who lived here in those years.
curiosities:Sanary, capital of German le.why: Read the 36 names on the plaque, then look at the quiet port they chose to wait in.
facts: The plaque with the 36 names, in the patio of the Sanary tourist office (town heritage guide); the town's exile heritage panels

The colony's span is given as 1933-1940, 1933-1942 or, on the plaque, 1933-1945; the regional tourism site says Brecht finished The Threepenny Opera in Sanary, but other sources place that 1928 work at Le Lavandou, years before the exile

provisioning:Cours Lafayette.name: Cours Lafayette market
provisioning:Cours Lafayette.teaser: A kilometre of fish, cheese and growers' crates, Tuesday to Sunday, packed away by half past twelve
provisioning:Cours Lafayette.story: For a cook this is Toulon's daily shop. Work the cours from the Place Louis Blanc end: the fishmongers first, while the ice is fresh, then the cheesemongers, the charcuterie and the Provençal growers with the week's vegetables. Buy the fish early and keep it cold, and leave the heavy produce for last so you carry less. The cade carts at that end have their own card.
provisioning:Cours Lafayette.why: Shop before ten for the fish; the food stalls pack up around half past twelve and only non-food stalls stay on.
facts: The day's fish, a local cheese, charcuterie and seasonal vegetables from the growers' stalls

provisioning:Sanary's Wednesday market.name: Sanary Wednesday market
provisioning:Sanary's Wednesday market.teaser: Wednesday on the port at Sanary: the big market under the plane trees, the fishing boats a few steps away
provisioning:Sanary's Wednesday market.story: Every Wednesday morning the stalls run along the port of Sanary-sur-Mer, under the plane trees of the Allées d'Estienne d'Orves, from about 8am until 1pm: tomatoes, tapenade, cade and chickpea galettes, cheese, flowers and the rest of a Provençal larder. In 2018 TF1 viewers voted it France's most beautiful market, a public vote for looks rather than a food award, and the crowds followed. The better buy is often separate: on Quai Charles de Gaulle the town's fishermen sell the morning catch straight off their little pointus, when the sea allows.

provisioning:The Aups truffle market.name: Aups truffle market
provisioning:The Aups truffle market.teaser: Thursday mornings in winter, Place Mistral in Aups trades black truffles until the baskets are empty
provisioning:The Aups truffle market.story: From late November the Haut-Var's truffle hunters bring the black winter truffle, Tuber melanosporum, to Place Frédéric Mistral in Aups every Thursday morning. The 2026-27 season opens on Thursday 26 November 2026 with a ceremony at 9am and is listed to run until 25 March 2027, though a poor year cuts it short, and selling stops once the truffles are gone, often well before noon. Smell before you buy. In January the town holds its Fête de la Truffe, with dog-and-handler hunting demonstrations, a producers' market and a charity truffle auction.

provisioning:Vieux Moulin du Partégal.teaser: A 16th-century olive mill east of Toulon where the guided tour and the tasting cost nothing
provisioning:Vieux Moulin du Partégal.story: The Vieux Moulin à huile du Partégal stands on the chemin des Laures at La Farlède, in the valley east of Toulon, and dates from the 16th century. The guided visit, in French or English, takes about an hour and a quarter: the old mill, how the olives become oil, then the tasting table, where several oils are poured side by side before tapenades and other local products. For a cook stocking a galley, it is the simplest way to taste Provençal oils against each other before choosing which bottles to buy.

provisioning:The Solliès fig growers.story: The Figue de Solliès is the violet-black Bourjassotte Noire, grown in the Gapeau valley around Solliès-Pont, east of Toulon. The harvest opens around 15 August, a second crop follows in September, and the last fruit comes in October, so mid-autumn is the tail of the season. Buy from village stalls and markets, where growers sell trays picked that morning: soft, heavy figs that should give slightly under the thumb. At the end of August the fig fair fills the centre of Solliès-Pont; its 29th edition, on 29 and 30 August 2026, drew about 150 exhibitors.
provisioning:The Solliès fig growers.why: Eat one at the stall and buy only what you will use within a day or two; ripe figs do not travel.

provisioning:Maison des Vins de Bandol.teaser: The appellation's own cellar below Le Castellet: Bandol reds and rosés side by side, with advisers to help
provisioning:Maison des Vins de Bandol.story: Despite the name, it is not in Bandol. The appellation's tasting cellar sits among the vines at the entrance to Le Castellet, on the chemin de la Ferrage. In Bandol town, the separate Oenothèque on Place Lucien Artaud also sells the appellation and receives growers mainly in July and August.

walks:Presqu'île de Giens & the salt pan.name: Presqu'île de Giens
walks:Presqu'île de Giens & the salt pan.teaser: Two sand bars tie Giens to the mainland, with flamingos standing in the old salt pans between them
walks:Presqu'île de Giens & the salt pan.story: Giens is an island that got caught. Two parallel sand bars, a rare double tombolo, fasten it to the coast at Hyères and enclose the old Salins des Pesquiers, where the Salins du Midi company made salt until 1995. The Conservatoire du littoral has owned the marsh since 2001, and pink flamingos stand in it all year, at their most numerous, around 2,000, in late summer. The path round the wild west and south shores follows the old customs patrols' beat, and a 1976 law keeps a three-metre strip along the French shore open to walkers, even across private land.
walks:Presqu'île de Giens & the salt pan.why: Walk the cliffs of the south shore with the wind in your face, then come back past the salt pans in the late light for the birds.

walks:The customs path, Gigaro to L'Esca.story: Long before the beach clubs, men in uniform walked this shore watching for smugglers. The sentier du littoral is often dated to 1791, the year the revolutionary state founded its customs service, though no source pins down when this stretch was first cut. Today it threads the protected capes between Gigaro, at La Croix-Valmer, and L'Escalet in Ramatuelle: up over Cap Lardier through cistus and heather, down to coves of coarse sand, round past Cap Taillat, which has its own card, with the sea working at the rocks below.

walks:Mont Faron.teaser: Six minutes by cable car above Toulon, and the whole roadstead lies at your feet
walks:Mont Faron.story: From the top of Mont Faron, 584 m above the town, the rade of Toulon is laid out whole: one of Europe's great natural roadsteads, the naval base with its grey hulls along the quays, ferries working in and out of the old port, and on a clear day the Massif de la Sainte-Baume on the skyline. The cable car climbs from Boulevard Amiral Vence in about six minutes. At the top, paths run along the limestone ridge between viewpoints, and a memorial to the August 1944 landings stands near the summit; its story is on its own card.

walks:Sentier Blanc-Martel.name: Sentier Blanc-Martel
walks:Sentier Blanc-Martel.teaser: Sixteen kilometres down through the Verdon gorge, with steel ladders and a 670 m tunnel in the dark
walks:Sentier Blanc-Martel.story: In August 1905 the speleologist Édouard-Alfred Martel, sent by the Ministry of Agriculture to look for drinking water for Provence, made the first full traverse of the Verdon gorge, guided by Isidore Blanc, the schoolmaster of Rougon. The Touring Club de France built the path between 1926 and 1928, ladders at the Brèche Imbert included, and Blanc worked on it until his accidental death in 1933; it has carried both names since 2005. It runs on the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence bank, down from the Chalet de la Maline to the river and out through unlit tunnels near the Couloir Samson.

walks:Up to the Chartreuse de la Verne.name: Chartreuse de la Verne
walks:Up to the Chartreuse de la Verne.teaser: A dark-stone monastery on a Maures ridge, founded around 1170 and silent again since 1983
walks:Up to the Chartreuse de la Verne.story: The Carthusians came to this ridge above the chestnut woods around 1170, under the bishops of Toulon and Fréjus, and their first church was consecrated on 3 October 1174. The lords of Bormes pillaged it in 1416; the Revolution confiscated it in 1789 and the monks left. The green-black serpentine framing its doorways was quarried nearby in the Maures. Listed as a historic monument since 1921, it has been home since 1983 to the nuns of the monastic Family of Bethlehem, so you visit the edges of a working silence, booklet in hand, with the forest close on every side.

calas:Plage Notre-Dame.teaser: Eight hundred metres of pale sand under the pines, on the Porquerolles bay that turns its back to the mistral
calas:Plage Notre-Dame.story: On 22 February 1912 François-Joseph Fournier, who had made his fortune from a gold lode in Mexico, bought almost all of Porquerolles at auction as a present for his wife Sylvia, then planted the eucalyptus, mimosa and umbrella pines that still shade its tracks. The French state bought most of the island in 1971. Notre-Dame is the long bay east of the village, about 800 m of pale sand with Aleppo pines growing almost to the water, angled so it is sheltered from both the mistral and the east wind. European Best Destinations named it Europe's most beautiful beach in 2015.

Below you are posidonia meadows, wrasse and grouper that do not bolt, because nobody has speared fish here for more than sixty years. Laid in 1979, it was France's first underwater trail.

calas:Cap Taillat.name: Cap Taillat
calas:Cap Taillat.teaser: A sand neck ties a scrubby islet to the shore, with a swim on either side of it
calas:Cap Taillat.story: Cap Taillat came close to being a holiday village. In 1970 a company bought 27 hectares here for 400 Club Med bungalows and a marina; Ramatuelle's mayor called in the Conservatoire du littoral, which bought the cape in 1987. What survived is a sand isthmus joining a scrubby islet to the shore, with clear water on both flanks, and on the ridge above it the Dolmen de Briande, a Neolithic tomb excavated in 1935, the southernmost in the Var. The maquis looks young because it is: the fire of 24 July 2017 burned some 550 hectares across Taillat and Cap Lardier.

calas:Pampelonne, the public end.story: Pampelonne runs about 4.5 km along the east side of the Ramatuelle peninsula, some 27 hectares of sand. For decades the clubs crept forward onto it. The sand is public. Spread a towel on the open stretches towards the Bonne Terrasse end or Tahiti, and walk past the clubs, which have their own cards.

avoid:Saint-Tropez in August.teaser: You picture Bardot's fishing port; August gives you traffic, a wall of yachts and a square you cannot cross
avoid:Saint-Tropez in August.story: The picture in your head is a fishing port. In August the roads in are jammed for hours, the old quay is walled with superyachts moored stern-to, the Place des Lices is too full to walk through, and the rosé is priced for the view. Nothing is wrong with the town; it is the wrong month. The same harbour at the end of September and into early October fills instead with classic yachts racing in Les Voiles de Saint-Tropez, the light is softer, and the summer crowd has gone home.

avoid:Eating on the photogenic quay.teaser: Photo menus and a host waving you in: on the harbour front you pay for the view, not the plate
avoid:Eating on the photogenic quay.story: The harbour-front terraces in Saint-Tropez, Sainte-Maxime and Cavalaire are easy to spot: laminated menus with photographs, a host on the pavement beckoning, the best view in town. You pay for that view, not for what arrives on the plate. The cooking the Var is proud of usually sits a street or two back from the water, or twenty minutes inland, in Maures villages such as Collobrières, La Garde-Freinet and Gassin, and in the wine hamlets around Bandol and La Londe, where locals eat for about half the price.

avoid:Thinking the Var stops at the beac.story: Most visitors never leave the strip along the sea, and so they miss the department's real larder: the truffle oaks of the Haut-Var, the chestnut woods of the Maures, and the Verdon gorge, cold water when the coast is roasting. Give the interior one whole day and time it to the calendar. This autumn that means Collobrières on a chestnut-festival Sunday; from late November, the Thursday-morning truffle market on Place Mistral in Aups, which has its own card.

culture:Villa Noailles.teaser: A white cubist house above Hyères where the Noailles paid for Buñuel, Man Ray and a garden in a triangle
culture:Villa Noailles.story: Charles and Marie-Laure de Noailles gave the young Robert Mallet-Stevens a slope above the old town and asked, so the story goes, for an interesting little house to live in. From 1923 to 1933 he kept adding to it: an indoor pool, a gymnasium, a squash court, terraces of white cubes. In 1926-27 Gabriel Guévrékian laid out the triangular Cubist garden of coloured tiles and squares of planting. They also paid for Buñuel's L'Âge d'or, and Man Ray filmed Les Mystères du Château de Dé here in 1929. Hyères bought the house in 1973; it is now an art centre for design, fashion, architecture and photography.
culture:Villa Noailles.why: Walk into the Cubist garden and look back at the house: the whole idea of a joyful modernism fits in one view.

culture:Fondation Carmignac.name: Fondation Carmignac
culture:Fondation Carmignac.teaser: Shoes off at the door, then galleries under a farmhouse and a ceiling of water on Porquerolles
culture:Fondation Carmignac.story: Édouard Carmignac, financier and collector, opened his foundation in 2018 under an old Provençal mas on Porquerolles. The 2,000 m² of galleries lie below ground, lit through a ceiling of water. Visitors leave their shoes at the entrance and walk the cool stone floors barefoot, then go out into fifteen hectares of garden with sculpture set among umbrella pines and vines. The island is part of the national park and has no visitor cars, so you come by ferry and walk or cycle up the track. culture:Domaine du Rayol.name: Domaine du Rayol
culture:Domaine du Rayol.teaser: Chilean matorral, South African fynbos and Californian chaparral, all on one Var slope facing Port-Cros
culture:Domaine du Rayol.story: Around 1910 a businessman, Alfred Courmes, built the estate and its great pergola above the sea. The aviation industrialist Henri Potez bought it in 1940 and cut the long stair down through cypresses to the water. Abandoned later, it was bought by the Conservatoire du littoral in 1989, which brought in the landscape gardener Gilles Clément. He refused clipped beds. Instead he planted the floras of the world's other Mediterranean climates, from Chile, California, South Africa and Australia, and let them seed and move. Seven of the twenty hectares are garden, the rest maquis, worked from the start without irrigation or pesticides.

culture:The Citadelle.name: The Citadelle
culture:The Citadelle.teaser: A six-sided keep of 1602-08 above the port, with the widest view of the gulf and the Maures
culture:The Citadelle.story: The keep went up between 1602 and 1608 on the hill behind the town, with ramparts that still look down on the harbour and across the gulf to Sainte-Maxime. Inside, the maritime history museum tells the story of Saint-Tropez sailors rather than yachts: the Bailli de Suffren, the fishing boats, and the coastal trade that kept thousands of local men at sea for centuries. The climb up through the old town is short and steep, and on a clear autumn day the Maures stand out sharp behind the water.

culture:Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption.name: Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption
culture:Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption.teaser: The ochre and sienna tower on every postcard, and inside, the gilded bust of Saint Torpes
culture:Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption.story: The town's parish church is Italian baroque, and its ochre and sienna bell tower is what you see first from the sea. Inside sits the gilded bust of Saint Torpes, the saint the town is named after. Every May, during the Bravade, it is carried out through the streets to musket volleys fired by townsmen in old uniform, the noisiest and most local three days of the Saint-Tropez year. The rest of the time the church is quiet and cool, a few lanes back from the quay.

culture:Musée de l'Annonciade.name: Musée de l'Annonciade
culture:Musée de l'Annonciade.teaser: A port chapel full of the colour Signac, Matisse and Bonnard found in Saint-Tropez
culture:Musée de l'Annonciade.story: Paul Signac sailed into Saint-Tropez in 1892 and stayed some twenty years. At his house, La Hune, he received Henri-Edmond Cross, Matisse, Marquet and others, and the port became a painters' place before it was a famous one. The town opened a museum in 1922. In 1950 the collector Georges Grammont was given a deconsecrated sixteenth-century chapel on the quay; the architect Louis Süe redesigned it, Grammont gave fifty-six works, and the new museum opened on 10 July 1955. The pictures run from about 1890 to 1950: pointillists, Nabis, Fauves, many of them painting the harbour just outside the door.

culture:Village des Tortues.name: Village des Tortues
culture:Village des Tortues.teaser: Walk among Hermann's tortoises, France's only native land tortoise, at the foot of the Maures
culture:Village des Tortues.story: The Maures and the Plaine des Maures hold the last wild population of Hermann's tortoise on the French mainland. In 1986 the naturalists Bernard Devaux and David Stubbs founded the SOPTOM association to save it, and on 28 May 1988 they opened the first tortoise village at Gonfaron. It moved to a two-hectare site at Carnoules in June 2017. Here you walk past the veterinary clinic, the incubators and the breeding pens, and watch small domed shells working through the dry grass. The animals' two great enemies are summer wildfire and the roads that slice up their range.

craft:Do this one.name: Atelier M.CO, Salernes
craft:Do this one.teaser: Throw a pot in Salernes clay, in the town that tiled Provence with red tomettes
craft:Do this one.story: Salernes, in the Haut-Var, lived for centuries on its red clay. Its kilns turned out the hexagonal terracotta tomettes laid in farmhouse kitchens across Provence, and the Terra Rossa museum, set up in an old tomette works on the edge of town, keeps the machines and more than 2,000 decorated tiles. The potter Marjorie Covlet still works the local earth at her Atelier M.CO, making tableware and decorative pieces in Salernes clay, to choose from or to order. She also runs courses for adults and workshops for children. This is the one Var craft we found where a named maker will put the clay in your own hands.

craft:Other one.name: Courrieu, Cogolin
craft:Other one.teaser: Briar pipes cut from Maures heather roots, made by one family since 1802
craft:Other one.story: Cogolin made its name on the tree heather of the Maures, whose dense root burl, the briar, will take a flame without burning. A guided visit of about an hour follows the work from grubbing the heather roots out of the hills to the finished, polished bowl, and the shop sells what the bench produces. Missing: a class; you watch and buy, but no one here teaches you to make a pipe.

craft:What is sold as Provençal craft.name: What is sold as Provençal craft
craft:What is sold as Provençal craft.teaser: 'Savon de Marseille' on a bar is not a protected name, and the soap makers have fought over it for years
craft:What is sold as Provençal craft.story: Anyone may stamp Savon de Marseille on soap. In 2015 and 2016 three rival associations filed specifications with France's industrial-property office, the INPI, to protect the name. The four makers of the UPSM, Fer à Cheval, Le Sérail and Du Midi in Marseille and Marius Fabre in Salon-de-Provence, argued for vegetable oils only, the traditional cauldron method, no additives and production in the Bouches-du-Rhône. Twelve rival firms wanted room for perfumes and colourings; a third group, asking for all of France, was refused. Without a settled label, a gift-shop cube can come from anywhere, and a 'Provence' print or sachet describes a style, not a place of making.
craft:What is sold as Provençal craft.why: Buy soap with a maker's name and town on it, and turn over any 'Provence' print or sachet for the line that says where it was made.
facts: Soap cubes stamped Savon de Marseille with no maker named; 'Provence' prints and lavender sachets with no place of manufacture on the label

linger:Cafés Magali.name: Cafés Magali
linger:Cafés Magali.teaser: A Toulon roaster since 1928 that went over to light, single-origin coffee and opened a counter to drink it
linger:Cafés Magali.story: Cafés Magali has roasted in Toulon since 1928 and was named best roaster in France in 2011. The change came in 2021, when Frédéric De Barros, who came from Café Mokxa in Lyon, took over the roasting and turned it toward café de spécialité: single origins, roasted light, nothing scorched. In 2025 the house finally opened a coffee-shop counter where you can taste the lots rather than just buy the bags. It is the place in the Var to have a filter coffee explained to you by the person who roasted it.

linger:Sénéquier.story: The name goes back to 1887, when Marie and Martin Sénéquier opened a pâtisserie on the Place aux Herbes, known for a white nougat of almonds, pistachios and Provence honey. In 1930 Lisette Sénéquier took the business to the harbour as a café and tea room. Bombed in 1944, it was rebuilt by 1951, and its thirty metres of scarlet chairs and triangular tables became the seat from which the New Wave, the fishermen and everyone since have watched the port. The coffee costs port prices; what you are paying for is the sightline over the whole quay.

drink:Bandol rouge.name: Bandol rouge
drink:Bandol rouge.teaser: Mourvèdre by law, eighteen months in wood by law: the one Var red made to wait a decade
drink:Bandol rouge.story: Bandol's rules make the red slow on purpose. At least half the blend must be Mourvèdre, and the wine spends a minimum of eighteen months in wood, mostly big old foudres, before it can be sold. Mourvèdre ripens late and only finishes properly on warm, sea-facing ground, which is what the Bandol terraces give it: a limestone and marl amphitheatre climbing from the coast, up to about 300 metres at Pibarnon. Opened young, it is tannic and closed, smelling of leather, black olive and garrigue more than fruit. Given ten years or more in bottle, the tannin softens and the fruit and spice come forward.
drink:Bandol rouge.why: Order a bottle at least eight to ten years old if the list has one, and ask for it decanted.

drink:Bandol rosé.name: Bandol rosé
drink:Bandol rosé.teaser: Deeper in colour and built on Mourvèdre, this is the rosé you pour with fish soup, not by the pool
drink:Bandol rosé.story: Bandol rosé shares the red's grape. Tempier's runs at roughly 55 percent Mourvèdre, which gives it more colour, grip and length than the pale pinks sold all along the coast. The American importer Kermit Lynch began shipping Tempier from the late 1970s, and for many wine drinkers abroad that bottle was the first proof that a Provençal rosé could be serious. It holds up to bouillabaisse, aïoli and even grilled lamb, and unlike most rosé it gains from a year in the cellar. The pale fashion bottles have their own warning card in the guide.

drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.name: Côtes de Provence rosé
drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.teaser: Pressed pale, dry and drunk young: the bottle on almost every table between Toulon and Saint-Tropez
drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.story: Côtes de Provence is the largest appellation in Provence, about 20,000 hectares, and close to nine bottles in ten it makes are rosé. The grapes are mostly Grenache, Cinsault and Syrah, with some Rolle, picked early and pressed quickly so the juice barely takes colour. The result should be bone-dry, cool and light. Quality runs from industrial to properly fine, and the price is no guide. It is made to be drunk in the year after the harvest: older bottles fade fast. For more depth at a lower price, look inland to Coteaux Varois en Provence around Brignoles.
drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.why: Ask for the most recent vintage, served very cold, and leave last year's bottle on the shelf.

drink:Pastis.name: Pastis
drink:Pastis.teaser: Anise, liquorice and herbs turned cloudy with cold water: the coast's evening ritual, made just next door
drink:Pastis.story: Pastis is not a Var drink, though the Var drinks plenty of it. Paul Ricard launched his in Marseille in 1932, one of many anise drinks that filled the gap after France banned absinthe in 1915. The method matters: about one part pastis to five of cold water, poured in that order, then ice, so the anethole turns the glass milky without clumping. Most bars pour Ricard or Pastis 51. For a glass where the herbs come through past the liquorice, ask for Henri Bardouin from Forcalquier, made with more than sixty plants and spices.
drink:Pastis.why: Ask for a Bardouin at the café bar and add the water yourself from the carafe.
facts: Clear amber turning cloudy yellow with water; star anise, liquorice, fennel, garrigue herbs

drink:Fleur de Figue.name: Fleur de Figue
drink:Fleur de Figue.teaser: A fig liqueur from Taradeau, drunk neat after dinner or splashed into cold rosé before it
drink:Fleur de Figue.story: Figs are a Var obsession, and the Solliès growers and their violet fig have their own cards in this guide. This liqueur, macerated and bottled in the Var at Taradeau, puts the fruit in a small glass: late summer, honeyed and dark. The Liquoristerie de Provence, the maker named for it, works by macerating and infusing real plants and fruit rather than adding synthetic flavour, and holds the state's Entreprise du Patrimoine Vivant label. around:Tourtour & Aups.teaser: A stone village at 635 metres with Sainte-Victoire on the skyline, and the truffle town ten kilometres away
around:Tourtour & Aups.story: Tourtour sits on a ridge at about 635 metres, high enough that the French call it the village dans le ciel, the village in the sky. It is one of the Plus Beaux Villages de France. From its edge on a clear day you see the Maures, the Sainte-Baume and the Montagne Sainte-Victoire, and sometimes as far as Mont Ventoux. About ten kilometres west on the D77 is Aups, a quiet stone town for most of the year that wakes up in winter as the market town of the Haut-Var's black truffle. The two villages make one drive: Tourtour for the view, Aups for the reason to come in winter.
around:Tourtour & Aups.why: Time it for a winter Thursday, when Aups holds its truffle market; out of season, go for the Tourtour view at the end of the day.
facts: About 1h15 to 1h30 by car north from the coast; Aups is about 10 km from Tourtour
Half a day, or a full day with Cotignac
The Tourtour viewpoints in clear weather; the Aups truffle market in season (its own card)
In either village; this guide lists no table there

around:Bandol wine country.name: Bandol wine country
around:Bandol wine country.teaser: Terraced vines between two hilltop villages, all turned to the sea, where Bandol's slow red grape ripens
around:Bandol wine country.story: Behind the port of Bandol the land rises in an amphitheatre of stone terraces, the restanques, between the hilltop villages of La Cadière-d'Azur and Le Castellet. They face south to the sea and trap the sun. That matters because the appellation's red is built on mourvèdre, a grape that ripens late and needs the heat to give its dark, savoury fruit. The best estates are tucked among these slopes: Domaine Tempier at Le Plan-du-Castellet, which did most to make Bandol a wine to age; Château de Pibarnon on its high bowl above La Cadière. Walk up into either village and you can see the whole slope at once.
around:Bandol wine country.why: Book one cellar-door tasting ahead, then walk the lanes of Le Castellet; the drink cards cover what to order.
facts: About 35 to 45 minutes by car west of Toulon
A half day for one tasting and one village; a full day with lunch
